text:
Not insane at all. Lots of full-time working couples have happy, well-adjusted dogs. It just takes more planning than people expect, and the dog you choose matters a lot.

## The full-time work question

**What matters most:**
- **How long the dog is actually alone.** A typical adult dog does okay with 4–6 hours alone. Eight to ten hours straight is rough for most dogs without a midday break.
- **Your schedules.** Do either of you work from home some days? Can you stagger your hours? Is one of you close enough to come home at lunch? Hybrid schedules make this much easier.
- **Budget for help.** A midday dog walker (often $20–35 per walk) or doggy daycare a few days a week ($30–60/day depending on area) can close the gap. Price this out before committing, because it can easily cost $400–800+/month.

**Puppy vs. adult:** This is probably your biggest decision. Puppies need to go out every 2–3 hours at first, need lots of training and socialization, and can't be left for long stretches. If you both work full-time in an office, **an adult dog (2+ years) is usually a much better fit.** Many rescues know their dogs' personalities well and can match you with one that's already house-trained and calm when alone.

**Energy level:** A low-to-moderate energy dog will happily sleep most of the day. A high-energy working breed (Border Collie, Malinois, many Huskies) left alone all day often becomes destructive or anxious.

## Things first-time owners often don't think about

**Time**
- Mornings get earlier. Most dogs need a real walk before you leave, not just a quick pee break.
- Training is ongoing, not a one-time class.
- The first few weeks are intense. If possible, take some time off or bring the dog home before a long weekend.

**Money**
- Vet costs beyond routine care: an emergency visit or surgery can run $1,000–5,000+. Look into pet insurance or set up a dedicated emergency fund.
- Food, preventatives (flea/tick/heartworm), grooming (some breeds need professional grooming every 6–8 weeks), toys, crate, bed, and replacing things they destroy.
- Boarding or a pet sitter every time you travel.

**Lifestyle**
- Spontaneous plans get harder. Last-minute dinner after work or a weekend trip now needs dog logistics.
- Housing: check your lease (pet fees, breed or weight restrictions) and think about future moves too.
- Dogs live 10–15+ years. Think about where you'll be: kids, moves, job changes.

**Relationship stuff (seriously worth discussing)**
- Who does the morning walk? Night walk? Vet appointments?
- Rules: Is the dog allowed on the couch? The bed?
- Training consistency: if one of you lets the dog jump up and the other doesn't, it confuses the dog.
- Is one of you more excited than the other? That's common, but be honest about it, because the less enthusiastic person often ends up resentful if they end up doing half the work.

**Behavioral surprises**
- Separation anxiety is real and can be hard to fix. Practicing short absences early helps.
- Rescue dogs often take about 3 days to decompress, 3 weeks to learn your routine, and 3 months to feel fully at home. Their personality may change over that time.

## Some ways to test the waters
- **Foster through a local rescue.** This is the best trial run there is: you experience real dog life with support, and you help a dog in the meantime.
- **Dog-sit** for a friend for a week.
- **Do a mock schedule** for a couple of weeks: get up early for a "walk," come home when you'd need to, and see how it feels.
- **Talk to rescues.** Good ones will ask about your schedule and suggest dogs that fit it.

If you tell me more, like your work schedules, living situation (apartment vs. house, yard?), how active you two are, and whether you're leaning toward a puppy or rescue, I can give more specific thoughts, including breeds or types of dogs that tend to suit working couples.
